BILL NUMBER:  S4110               REVISED 05/08/09

 TITLE OF BILL :

An act to amend the labor law, in relation to unemployment insurance
benefits and part-time work, voluntary separations from employment,
and on/off indicators for extended unemployment insurance benefits;
and in relation to extended benefits


 PURPOSE :

The purpose of this bill is to conform New York's unemployment
insurance law to federal law so that the State may use federal funds
to provide extended unemployment benefits to New Yorkers whose
benefits will otherwise expire.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :

Section 1 of the bill would amend Labor Law § 593(1) to allow the
state to provide federally-funded unemployment benefits for
individuals who leave work for compelling family reasons and who are
currently eligible for benefits under state case law and statutes, by
conforming the language of state law to federal law.

Sections 2 and 3 of the bill would amend Labor Law §593(2) and §596(5)
to provide that individuals who work part-time and unwilling or unable
to work full-time would not be disqualified from receiving benefits if
they refuse to accept full-time employment.

Section 4 of the bill would make the following changes to Labor Law
§601:

* Labor Law §601(1)( a) would be amended to create a new unemployment
rate trigger, known as the "total unemployment rate (TUR)," to make
New York eligible for federally-funded unemployment benefits whenever
Congress provides 100% reimbursement for benefits.
* Labor Law §601(1)(a)(2) would be amended to provide that a "state
off indicator" would end the trigger if the conditions creating it no
longer exist.
* Labor Law §601(1)(a)(4) would be added to provide a definition for
the TUR trigger.
* Labor Law §601(1)(b) would be amended to extend the UI eligibility
period to include the alternate eligibility period provided by federal
law.
* The definitions for "extended benefits" and "regular benefits" would
be amended to conform to federal law.
* Labor Law §601(2)(t) would be amended to conform language regarding
earning requirements to federal law.
* Labor Law §601(3) would be amended to provide additional benefits
during "periods of high unemployment," where Congress provides 100%
sharing of the benefit costs.
* Labor Law §601(4) would be amended to conform UI benefit charging
for Indian tribes to federal law, and to charge the benefit costs for
a federal extended benefit program to the UI general account.
* Labor law §601(5) would be amended to conform state law to federal
law which excludes individuals from work search requirements if they
are receiving unemployment benefits while in approved training
programs, and to conform state law concerning work requirements to
reestablish eligibility for unemployment.

Section 7 of the bill establishes the effective date.

 EXISTING LAW :


Labor Law § 593(1) provides that a voluntary separation from
employment may be with good cause if the separation resulted from
circumstances where the claimant was a victim of domestic violence.

Labor Law § 593(2) provides that a claimant shall not be ineligible
for unemployment benefits as a consequence of refusing to accept
employment under certain circumstances.

Labor Law § 596(5) provides that a claimant who is unable or unwilling
to work full-time and customarily works less than the usual full time
hours at his place of employment, shall register as a short time
worker and be considered to have worked a full-time week.

Labor Law § 601 provides that a state "on indicator" to trigger
extended benefits must be based on state's Insured Unemployment Rate
(IUR), which may be federally reimbursed at a 50% rate.

Labor Law § 601(1)(a)(4) defines "eligibility period" as the period
beginning within an extended benefit period until the end of that
period.

Labor Law § 601(2)(f) provides that a claimant must have twenty weeks
of full-time employment or remuneration equal to 40 times his most
recent benefit rate to qualify for extended benefits.

Labor Law § 601(4) provides that governmental entities that do not
contribute to the Unemployment Trust Fund must assume the cost of
extended benefits.

 PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :

This is a new proposal.

 JUSTIFICATION :

This legislation would provide an additional 13 weeks of unemployment
benefits to approximately 120,000 New Yorkers who are out of work.
Congress recently approved 33 weeks of extended unemployment benefits
beyond the 26 weeks of regular benefits allowed under state law, but
these extended benefits will start to run out in mid-May. Unless this
legislation is adopted, 56,000 New Yorkers will lose their
unemployment benefits at that time, and an additional 5,000 to 8,000
will exhaust their benefits in each following week. If their benefits
are not continued, the impact on local governments statewide will be
immediate since the potential exists for these New Yorkers to enter
the social services system at once. Since UI benefits are the only
source of income for many unemployed workers, the failure to provide
benefits will also impact local economies. Studies show that every
dollar paid to workers returns approximately $1.64 to local businesses
from spending on food, rent and other basic needs.

New York is eligible to receive more than $600 million in federal
funds for unemployment benefits and administration approved by
Congress under the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009
(ARRA). In order to qualify, the state unemployment law must conform
to ARRA language concerning eligibility for benefits for separation
from employment due to compelling family reasons, including domestic
violence, the illness or disability of an immediate family member, or
the need to accompany the individual's spouse to a new location of
employment. Each of these compelling reasons have long been recognized
under well established state case law and statutes and would not
create new grounds for benefit eligibility in New York.

This bill would also create an alternate trigger to provide an
additional thirteen weeks of extended benefits to New Yorkers by using
the state's total unemployment rate (TUR).  Currently, the state
trigger is based on the average weekly number of individuals filing
claims for benefits, known as the uninsured rate of employment (IUR).
The TUR would apply only when Congress has appropriated funds to pay
100% of the costs of extended benefits. New York's most recently
calculated TUR meets the federal threshold, but the IUR falls short
and it is not expected to trigger on this year.  An amendment to the
state law is needed to include the TUR allow New York to receive 100%
reimbursement for extended benefits under the ARRA.

In light of current economic conditions, the State must do all it can
to deliver UI benefits to the unemployed, and make maximum use of all
funds available to meet its UI costs.

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :

The changes proposed in this legislation will bring an estimated $645
million in new federal funding to New York to cover the costs of UI
benefits, extended benefits, and the administration of the State UI
system. There would be a $4 million cost to the state for any benefits
which are not federally funded under the ARRA.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
This proposal would take effect immediately upon enactment.

BILL NUMBER:  S4110A          REVISED 05/18/09

 TITLE OF BILL :
An act to amend the labor law, in relation to unemployment insurance
benefits and part-time work, voluntary separations from employment,

and in relation to extended benefits


 PURPOSE :
To conform New York's unemployment insurance law to federal law to
allow the state to use federal funds to provide extended benefits to
New Yorkers whose unemployment benefits will otherwise expire, and to
provide additional federal money for the Unemployment Insurance Trust
Fund.

the TUR trigger.

* Labor Law §601(1)(b) would be amended to extend the UI eligibility

* The definitions for "extended benefits" and "regular benefits" would

* Labor Law §601(2)(t) would be amended to conform language regarding

programs, and to conform state law concerning work requirements to
reestablish eligibility for unemployment.
Section 7 of the bill establishes the effective date.

 EXISTING LAW :
Labor Law § 593(1} provides that a voluntary separation from
employment may be with good cause if the separation resulted from
circumstances where the claimant was a victim of domestic violence.
Labor Law § 593(2} provides that a claimant shall not be ineligible
for unemployment benefits as a consequence of refusing to accept
employment under certain circumstances.  Labor Law § 596(5} provides
that a claimant who is unable or unwilling to work full-time and
customarily works less than the usual full time hours at his place of
employment, shall register as a short time worker and be considered to
have worked a full-time week.  Labor Law § 601 provides that a state
"on indicator" to trigger extended benefits must be based on state's
Insured Unemployment Rate (IUR), which may be federally reimbursed at
a 50% rate.  Labor Law § 601(1}(a)(4) defines "eligibility period" as
the period beginning within an extended benefit period until the end
of that period.  Labor Law § 601(2}(f) provides that a claimant must

Labor Law § 601(4} provides that governmental entities that do not
contribute to the Unemployment Trust Fund must assume the cost of
extended benefits.

 PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :
This is a new proposal.

 JUSTIFICATION :
New York is eligible to receive more than $600 million in federal
funds for unemployment benefits and administration approved by
Congress under the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009
(ARRA). This legislation would allow the state to use part of these
funds to provide an additional 13 weeks of unemployment benefits to
approximately 120,000 New Yorkers who are out of work.  Previously,
Congress approved 33 weeks of extended unemployment benefits beyond
the 26 weeks of regular benefits allowed under state law, but these
extended benefits will start to run out in mid-May.  Unless this
legislation is adopted, 56,000 New Yorkers will lose their
unemployment benefits at that time, and an additional 5,000 to 8,000
will exhaust their benefits in each week after that. If these benefits
are not continued, the impact on local governments statewide will be
immediate since the potential exists for many of these New Yorkers to
enter the social services system at once. Since unemployment benefits
are the only Source of income for many unemployed workers, the failure
to provide benefits will also impact local economies. Studies show
that every dollar paid to workers returns approximately $1.64 to local
businesses from spending on food, rent and other basic needs.  This
bill would also create an alternate trigger to allow New York to
receive federal funds for extended benefits whenever Congress
appropriates 100% reimbursement for extended benefits. The alternative
trigger would be based on the state's total unemployment rate (TUR).
Currently, the state trigger is based uninsured rate of employment
(IUR) , which is limited to the average weekly number of individuals
filing claims. New York's most recently calculated TUR meets the
federal threshold, but the IUR falls short and is not expected to
trigger on this year. An amendment to the state law is needed to
include the TUR to allow New York to receive 100% reimbursement for
extended benefits under the ARRA.  In addition, the bill would provide
several hundred million dollars to the Unemployment Insurance Trust
Fund which pays benefits to unemployed workers. The Fund is currently
insolvent. New York has had to borrow money from the federal
government for which state interest is owed. In order to qualify for
these funds, the state unemployment law must conform to ARRA language
to allow individuals to receive benefits when they voluntarily
separate from employment for compelling family reasons, including
domestic violence, the illness or disability of an immediate family
member, and the need to accompany the individual's spouse to a new
location of employment.  Each of these compelling reasons has long
been recognized under state case law and statutes, and would not

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :
The changes proposed in this legislation will bring an estimated $645
million in new federal funding to New York to Cover the costs of UI
benefits, extended benefits, and the administration of the State UI
system. The bill would increase costs on the State and localities
during 2009 for which benefits are not federally funded under ARRA, by
$4 million and $24 million respectively. These added costs will be
offset, in part, by increased tax revenue from recipients of UI
benefits.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
This proposal would take effect immediately upon enactment.

summary: Relates to voluntary separations from work for compelling family reasons and to extended benefits; includes additional criteria for providing benefits in the case of voluntary separation; and provides extended unemployment benefits for certain periods.
